articles.title: Poll: Nearly 30% of Democrats would choose Harris for 2028
articles.summary: (The Center Square) – Democrats continue to favor former Vice President Kamala Harris over 12 other candidates if the 2028 Democratic presidential primary we...
articles.body:
(The Center Square) – Democrats continue to favor former Vice President Kamala Harris over 12 other candidates if the 2028 Democratic presidential primary were held today, according to The Center Square Voters' Voice Poll.

The Center Square has conducted four 2028 presidential primary polls since October, and Harris has retained about 30% of her party's support each time, though the October poll was her best. In the fall of 2025, 33% of registered Democrat and left-leaning Independent respondents indicated they would choose Harris from a list of eight prominent Democratic politicians. By March, when The Center Square added five more party leaders to the list, her support dipped to 31%. In June and August, she remained the Democratic favorite among 27% and 28% of respondents, respectively. She does appear to fare better among Democrats than left-leaning Independents, at 30% and 20% in August.

The most notable change among the other potential contenders is that support for the second-most-popular candidate, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, fell substantially with the addition of more options in March – from 21% to 16% – and he has plateaued in recent months at 14%. Meanwhile, former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg, who initially polled at 7%, climbed to 11% in June and then 12% in the August poll.

While Harris polled best in almost every major demographic group surveyed, she was most popular among the youngest voters and Black voters. Forty-seven percent of registered voters ages 18-29 preferred Harris to other prominent Democrats, and no one came close to her 49% among Black voters. Newsom came in a distant second among Black voters at10%.

Each polled racial demographic besides whites strongly favored Harris. She captured 30% of Hispanic and Latino respondents and 37% of respondents who identified as a race other than white, Black, Hispanic or Latino. She was still the most popular candidate among white voters at 18%, but Buttigieg was right behind at 17%, followed by Newsom at 16%.

Harris also fared slightly better among women than men, and was better among respondents with less formal education. She led among urban, suburban and rural voters, posting her strongest numbers among urban voters, and led across all four regions of the U.S., with her best showing in the South.

While Harris held a commanding lead over Newsom and Buttigieg among female voters, her advantage narrowed among men, where Newsom came within 10 points of her.

Newsom and Buttigieg also gained support among older demographics. Buttigieg was the favorite among senior voters. Buttigieg nabbed 20% support of the 65-and-older bracket; Newsom, 19% and Harris, 13%.

Buttigieg also bested Harris among respondents with post-graduate degrees, with 18% support to Harris' 15%.

New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has been included in the poll since March and while she generally came in after Newsom and Buttigieg, she was the second-most-popular choice among the 18-29 demographic with 13% support. She was also the second choice among Hispanic and Latino voters, with 17%. She polled better than Newsom with Independents (10% to his 9%) and better than Buttigeig in the Western region of the U.S. (11% to his 9%).

The Voters Voice Poll, conducted Aug. 12-16, surveyed 2,533 registered voters via opt-in online panel and text-to-web cell phone messages. The respondents were comprised of 930 Republicans, 930 Democrats and 673 Independents. Among independent voters, 330 respondents were classified as true independents, which are individuals who do not lean toward either major party when given the choice. The margin of error is +/- 2.0%.

articles.title: Tim Scott calls support for Darline Graham an ‘easy choice’ despite her debate flub
articles.summary: In an interview with “Meet the Press,” Scott defended Graham after her recent debate blunder raised questions about her qualifications.
articles.body: Sen. Tim Scott defended Sen. Darline Graham, his fellow South Carolina Republican, on Sunday ahead of her special GOP primary runoff this week, dismissing concerns about her debate blunder on national security last week. “Darline Graham is the real deal,” Scott told NBC News’ “Meet the Press,” adding that she is “highly qualified, incredibly competent, ready for primetime.” Asked how confident he is that Graham will win Tuesday’s primary runoff, Scott said, “Very confident,” adding that he waited several weeks before he endorsed her “to make sure that I felt like she was ready.” “I can tell you, as the senior senator for the great state of South Carolina, the person I want in the Senate with me, Darline Graham, representing the people of South Carolina,” he said. “Easy choice.” Scott boosted Graham just days after her viral moment at a debate against Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., whom she faces in Tuesday’s runoff. Asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are important national security issues facing the U.S., Graham answered: “I’m just going to be honest here. I’m not, on national security, I’m not that informed on national security, so, but I do support the military.” She added: “My brother was in the Air Force for 33 years, so I will do everything I can to support the military. My dad was in the Army. I’m not a polished politician up here. National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise. But I do support the military.” The answer drew concerns from some Republicans about Graham’s readiness to govern on national security and foreign policy issues — which were of pre-eminent concern for her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C. — if she’s elected to a full term. Darline Graham was appointed last month to serve the rest of her brother’s term after he died unexpectedly. Several days after she was appointed, Graham decided to run in a special election to serve a full term and was quickly endorsed by President Donald Trump. After the special primary election, in which Graham and Norman advanced to a runoff, Scott endorsed her, as well. Trump and Scott rallied in South Carolina in support of Graham’s campaign Friday, with Trump telling voters: “She only knows how to put America first. ... You vote for her, you’re going to be very proud of that vote.” On Sunday, Scott, who is chair of the Senate Republicans’ campaign arm, the National Republican Senatorial Committee, also spoke about competitive general election contests in states like Texas, Michigan and Iowa coming up in November. He defended the NRSC’s rhetoric about Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who would become the first Muslim senator if he is elected. The NRSC has repeatedly referred to El-Sayed’s faith in social media posts and alleged he has “terrorist ties” despite the lack of any evidence for the claim, drawing criticism from Democrats that Republicans are inciting Islamophobia. In an interview on “Meet the Press” this month, El-Sayed responded to GOP attacks painting him as “too radical,” saying, “We always knew they were going to go here.” “At the end of the day, it’s not radical to believe that people should be able to afford their groceries. It’s not radical to believe that you should have healthcare in this country,” he said. “Now, they’re going to try and paint me as a certain thing, given my name, but I also think it’s important for us to recognize that America has a long history of embracing,” he added. “America is a lot bigger than very small people.” Scott on Sunday pointed to El-Sayed’s decision to campaign in the primary with Hasan Piker, a Twitch streamer who once apologized for comments he made about the U.S. deserving the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. “Birds of a feather flock together,” Scott told “Meet the Press.” “The company you keep does matter.” Scott added that even though El-Sayed has denounced Piker’s past comments, he has not said he would stop campaigning with him. “You can’t denounce it with your words and do something different with your actions,” Scott said. “We believe what you do, not just what you say.” Speaking about the Senate race in Texas, which is a competitive contest between GOP state Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, Scott denounced Talarico as “weird” and “radical.” He also demurred when he was asked about concerns about Paxton’s character and his past, which includes an investigation by the Justice Department into whether he abused his office to aid a political donor and a 2023 vote by the GOP-led Texas House to impeach him. Paxton, who denied any wrongdoing and said the allegations were politically motivated, did not face any charges following the Justice Department investigation, and he was acquitted in a state Senate trial following his impeachment. Scott, who endorsed Paxton’s opponent, Sen. John Cornyn, in the GOP primary this year, did not respond when he was asked whether Paxton has the character to serve in the Senate. Instead, he denounced Talarico, saying: “I can tell you this: What we know with great clarity is that James Talarico does not have the character to serve in the United States Senate, nor does he have the ... right position on the issues that Texans care most about. I’ll say it very clearly, and I’ll say it again: James Talarico is out of step, completely out of step with Texans.” Talarico has called the GOP attacks a distraction aimed at drawing attention from the allegations against Paxton, and he has emphasized his legislative record and what he said was a focus on bipartisanship as a state lawmaker. “I’ve served for four terms in the Texas House of Representatives, where I brought Democrats and Republicans together to pass 60 bipartisan bills to cut property taxes, to raise teacher pay, to lower the cost of housing, childcare, prescription drugs, including insulin, and I’ve called out the extremes in both parties,” he said in an interview with NBC News in May.

articles.title: Sen. Chris Van Hollen says he’s ‘kicking the tires’ on a potential 2028 presidential bid
articles.summary: The Maryland Democrat also said on “Meet the Press” that democratic socialists have a place in the party “as part of the debate.”
articles.body: Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., said in an interview on NBC’s “Meet the Press” that he’s “kicking the tires” on a potential 2028 presidential bid. “We need to be against the status quo, and that’s why I’ve been kicking the tires as I look at 2028, because I don’t think the Democratic Party has answered the call about how we’re going to make sure we have an economy that really does work for everybody, especially working people,” he said. Van Hollen’s comments came as he was pressed about whether he is interested in challenging Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., as the chamber’s party leader, if Democrats retake the Senate this fall. Asked by moderator Kristen Welker whether he was interested in the position, Van Hollen said his focus was “not on majority leader, it’s on what Democrats stand for going into 2028.” Van Hollen, a longtime member of Congress, has been a prominent critic of the Trump administration and has pushed Democrats to provide a clear alternative to the Republican Party’s agenda. He has previously said he is “kicking the tires” in considering a potential 2028 run, acknowledging the possibility of a presidential campaign to NOTUS and at the Hill Nation Summit, an annual event put on by The Hill and NewsNation. Asked to clarify on “Meet the Press” whether his “kicking the tires” comments meant he was thinking about running, he noted that he has been to New Hampshire and Iowa, which have historically been the first two nominating states. In 2028, New Hampshire will still be an early nominating state, but Iowa was pushed out of the early window. “I think there’s a great deal of churning within the Democratic Party, and I support that,” he said. “As I said, I think we need this healthy debate, because I don’t think Democrats have put forward a clear alternative to the Trump administration.” Pushed again about whether he was considering running for president, he said, “Democrats need to be very clear not just what we’re against, but what we’re for.” “I very much want to be part of that debate, and I am kicking the tires, testing the waters,” he said. Several other Democrats have appeared open to running for president in 2028 in what could be a wide field of candidates, with no clear potential front-runner. California Gov. Gavin Newsom has said he would be “lying” if he denied he was considering a presidential campaign. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear has said he may “take a look” at running. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg said in an interview on “The Diary of a CEO” podcast that he doesn’t know whether he will run but that he is “more inclined than not.” Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., has said she hasn’t “ruled out the possibility.” Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., also has not ruled out a run, and Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., said he would “have to look at” the possibility. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, too, has said she is “thinking about” running for president again. Van Hollen was also asked on “Meet the Press” whether he believes democratic socialists should have a place in the Democratic Party. He said, “They do, as part of the debate.” “I’m not afraid to debate,” he added. “I think that those in the Democratic Party who are afraid of a healthy debate are missing the point because voters, including Democratic voters, they don’t want to simply return to the pre-Trump status quo. They want Democrats who are going to stand for something, and I can strongly disagree with one set of Democrats. But I think that debate is healthy.” Multiple democratic socialists have won primaries this cycle, most recently Angie Nixon, who won the Florida Democratic primary for the Senate last week. Nixon is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, a group whose platform includes replacing “the president and Supreme Court with an executive and judiciary chosen by and subordinate to Congress” and abolishing the Senate. Asked whether those platform points went too far for him, Van Hollen said, “Of course.” “Yes, of course they do for me, and I think a lot of the folks who are running, regardless of where they are on the Democratic spectrum, have rejected those ideas,” he said. Van Hollen served in the House for more than a decade before he was sworn in as senator in 2017.

articles.title: Scott: ‘There’s no doubt’ Darline Graham is qualified to be senator
articles.summary: Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) said Sunday that “there’s no doubt” his fellow South Carolina Republican Darline Graham is qualified to be a senator after her recent debate slip-up on an answer about national security. “Sen. Scott, is Darline Graham qualified to be a U.S. senator?” NBC News’s Kristen Welker asked Scott during his “Meet the…
articles.body:
Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) said Sunday that “there’s no doubt” his fellow South Carolina Republican Darline Graham is qualified to be a senator after her recent debate slip-up on an answer about national security.

“Sen. Scott, is Darline Graham qualified to be a U.S. senator?” NBC News’s Kristen Welker asked Scott during his “Meet the Press” appearance Sunday.

“Well, there’s no doubt, Kristen. Darlene Graham is the real deal,” Scott responded, adding later that Graham “is ready to take on the issues that everyday Americans are facing.”

“One other thing that’s really important: I watched her on the campaign trail. I watched her go through two funerals for her brother, and then I watched her carefully for 30 days in the Senate, casting deciding votes for the [attorney general], working on getting her first bill passed, the Russia sanctions bill. What did I assess? Highly qualified, incredibly competent, ready for prime time,” Scott said.

On Friday, President Trump defended Graham after she said during the South Carolina GOP Senate primary debate earlier this week that she is “not that informed on national security” but supports “the military.” She had been asked if Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues for the U.S.

Trump gave his support to the South Carolina senator as he was headed to Myrtle Beach, S.C., where he rallied alongside her later Friday, only a few days prior to the state’s Republican runoff.

The president has endorsed Graham since she was appointed to finish the rest of her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham’s (R-S.C.), term.

“She’s very smart, and she was being honest. She’s into the price of groceries. … She is going to do what the military wants, and really what the president wants,” Trump said Friday before leaving for South Carolina.

“She understands that national security is my thing. … I thought it was a very honest answer,” the president continued.

articles.title: Too sick to work? States must get their new Medicaid rules right.
articles.summary: Cancer doesn’t wait for a billing code to catch up. Neither should the states now deciding what counts as proof of illness.
articles.body:
Starting Jan. 1, 2027 , Illinois will ask adults in its Medicaid expansion program to either prove they worked 80 hours in the last month or that they are too sick to work. The state will answer that second question mostly with billing codes.

For a woman between an abnormal mammogram and a confirmed diagnosis, the billing codes say she is fine. Her doctors do not.

Congress set the requirement. States decide how to run it. The hardest decision is how you tell from a claims file who is too sick to work. On July 30, a federal judge declined to pause the rule while a multistate challenge proceeds. States are building their systems now — Illinois shows what is at stake in getting it wrong.

The law exempts people who are “medically frail,” a category meant to protect those with conditions that keep them from working. Cancer treatment can qualify, for example. The problem is how states find those patients.

Illinois, like most states, will lean on claims data, the billing codes generated when patients receive care. Those codes work well for a patient mid-chemotherapy, but they fail at both ends — both before a diagnosis is confirmed and after treatment ends while monitoring continues.

An abnormal mammogram creates a patient before it creates a diagnosis. Between the image and the pathology report, she moves through more imaging, a biopsy and specialists. The cancer code belongs to the end of that process. Until pathology confirms malignancy, the record holds only fragments: screening, abnormal finding, follow-up.

That is not how she experiences the interval. She is not waiting for a code. She is waiting to learn whether the shadow on the image is cancer.

If her Medicaid renewal falls in that window, the system reads the absence of a confirmed diagnosis as the absence of a serious condition. She has no diagnosis that qualifies her for an exemption. The record isn’t merely behind her illness, it is governing her access to care before the illness exists on its terms.

There’s a second trap, and it’s worse. Illinois covers breast and cervical cancer treatment through a separate Medicaid category , but the state’s own rules are explicit that people already eligible for Medicaid cannot receive benefits under it . A woman already enrolled through the expansion doesn’t move into that pathway when she’s diagnosed. She stays in the expansion group, subject to the work requirement, through surgery and chemotherapy. The exposure isn’t a gap of a few weeks before diagnosis — it’s a standing condition that lasts the length of her treatment.

Arkansas already ran this experiment. In the first seven months of its 2018 work requirement, about 18,000 people lost coverage , a full one in four of those subject to it. A study in the New England Journal of Medicine found employment did not rise. People lost coverage because they couldn’t navigate the reporting, not because they weren’t working. By early 2019, only about one in 10 had gotten it back.

The federal law is settled. The implementation isn’t, and states are already choosing differently: screening for medical frailty at application, building hardship exemptions, setting longer compliance periods. Illinois doesn’t need to redesign federal policy to protect these patients. It needs to decide where it puts the burden of proof.

What would protecting them look like? States could shield patients from the moment they get abnormal screening results, so they are not asked to prove they are sick during the weeks the record cannot yet show it.

States could add a grace period when a diagnosis is documented but the claim has not yet caught up. They could accept a letter from free or community clinics that don’t bill Medicaid, so the poorest patients aren’t invisible. They could keep survivors covered while they are still being monitored.

None of that changes the federal requirement; all of it is within the states’ power.

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services itself projects that 2.3 million people will lose Medicaid in the first year. No vote in Springfield will revisit the federal law. But in administrative offices over the coming months, officials will decide which diagnoses count, when exemptions begin, and how much proof patients must produce before the system believes they are sick.

Cancer doesn’t wait for a billing code to catch up. Neither should the states now deciding what counts as proof of illness.

Akshaya Sahasra Ganji is an undergraduate health policy researcher at Florida International University in a combined medical degree program. Her research focuses on women’s health, neuroscience and health policy.

articles.title: No more sunsets before 5 p.m.? How permanent daylight saving would change winter
articles.summary: A sunset after 7 p.m. in winter? That could be the reality for some.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – As the end of daylight saving time grows ever nearer (it’s happening as early as possible this year ), President Trump has continued his push to have the Senate pass a bill that would lock the clocks .

If daylight saving time were to become permanent, winters could feel different for many of us.

Under the Sunshine Protection Act, states that do not exempt themselves would observe daylight saving time year-round. Since Hawaii and most of Arizona already observe year-round standard time , they would remain exempt.

Outside of those two states, sunrises and sunsets would happen later than they currently do between early November and March.

In much of the U.S., the sun wouldn’t rise until after 8 a.m. for at least part of the winter. For some, the sun wouldn’t come up until after 9 a.m.

The trade-off, though, would be later sunsets in winter.

Depending on where you live, many winter sunsets may happen in the 4 or 5 o’clock hours. If our clocks did not fall back an hour in November, as they have done for years, those sunsets would shift to the 5 and 6 o’clock hours, respectively.

You may even be privy to a sunset after 7 p.m. — something we don’t see during winter now.

The interactive table below shows how many winter days you would see sunsets after 6 p.m. (or 7 p.m., for some) if permanent daylight saving time were to take effect. You can also view the latest winter sunset each city would experience under permanent daylight saving time. (In all cases, this occurs the day before clocks “spring forward” an hour.)

Though it isn’t displayed on the table above, Juneau would see its 40 sunsets that currently occur in the 3 p.m. hour shift back to the 4 o’clock hour.

Cities that currently see a large chunk of winter sunsets in the 4 o’clock hour now would see that slide back to the 5 o’clock hour. For cities like Green Bay and Burlington, Vermont, which each experience more than 90 winter sunsets before 5 p.m, the change could be well-received.

Juneau, Indianapolis and Louisville, Kentucky, would have some of the latest possible sunsets, all coming after 7:40 p.m. in early March. They would, however, receive the brunt of the less-desirable part of permanent daylight saving time: late winter sunrises .

While not as late as Juneau (the latest winter sunrise there would be after 11 a.m.), Indianapolis and Louisville would have sunrises as late or later than 9 a.m. for at least part of winter. Grand Rapids would have one of the latest sunrises in the country at 9:14 a.m.

It’s the late sunrises that contributed to the downfall of permanent daylight saving time in the past. It could negatively impact your health , disrupt how thousands practice their religion , and have “considerable implications” on your future flights , at least temporarily.

The House already passed the Sunshine Protection Act of 2026, but the Senate is on recess until September. It’s unclear, though, if the Senate will take up the legislation or if it has enough votes to pass and make daylight saving time permanent.

Congress is also considering two bills in the House that would give states the option to observe year-round daylight saving time, as well as a bill to make half-daylight saving time permanent , and a bill to make standard time permanent , with exceptions.

articles.title: Bitter Oklahoma governor’s runoff tests Trump’s endorsement power
articles.summary: President Trump faces one of the last major primary tests of his endorsement power on Tuesday in Oklahoma, where his pick for governor is battling in a tough runoff. His pick, Republican Mike Mazzei, finished less than a percentage point behind rival Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond (R) in the initial June GOP primary, as a…
articles.body:
President Trump faces one of the last major primary tests of his endorsement power on Tuesday in Oklahoma, where his pick for governor is battling in a tough runoff.

His pick, Republican Mike Mazzei, finished less than a percentage point behind rival Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond (R) in the initial June GOP primary, as a divided field kept either from winning outright.

As the runoff approaches, Trump has doubled down against Drummond in hopes that Mazzei, a former state senator and state budget secretary, can make it over the finish line in the red state, where the primary winner is all but assured to win the governor’s mansion this fall.

Along with the special runoff for Senate in South Carolina the same day, Oklahoma marks one of the final midterm primary gauges of the president’s political power amid his lackluster approval numbers — and it comes after five of his gubernatorial picks in open primaries lost so far this cycle.

“This is a classic test,” said Seth McKee, a political science professor at Oklahoma State University. “Because this endorsement is doing the heavy lifting in this race.”

Trump’s decision to back Mazzei came as a surprise to some, after signs that Drummond and other Republicans were poised to be front-runners for the seat being vacated by term-limited Gov. Kevin Stitt (R), teeing up the first wide-open Republican primary since 2018.

“It’s really this test of: Can a Trump endorsement get a dud over the finish line?” McKee said.

“I think we were all a little bit shocked when we saw that Trump endorsed Mazzei on this one. That moved him clearly into front-runner status, and it happened at a time when the other campaigns were attacking each other, and not really Mazzei,” said Tyler Powell, an Oklahoma-based political adviser who is not involved in the gubernatorial race. “So Mazzei kind of came in slightly unscathed into the race with the momentum.”

Since then, Mazzei’s “been purely relying on the Trump endorsement” as his pitch to voters, Powell argued, “and I think Oklahoma voters were getting turned off.”

Trump’s endorsement had already drawn scrutiny after revelations that Mazzei’s campaign paid nearly $70,000 to Trump confidante Roger Stone for consulting services, prompting critics to question whether the money factored into Trump’s decision.

Mazzei has pushed back against those claims, and his campaign has stressed that it was his staunch alignment with Trump that got him the nod.

But Trump’s support , which came just two weeks before the initial June primary, wasn’t enough to lock up the nomination. Against more than half a dozen other rivals, Mazzei finished a hair behind Drummond. The pair each notched roughly a quarter of the vote.

“Drummond had been the front-runner for quite some time, and so I think that’s really why Mazzei’s in the position he is, is because the Trump endorsement elevated him,” said Oklahoma Republican strategist and pollster Pat McFerron.

But Trump isn’t just backing Mazzei — he’s warning Oklahoma Republicans off Drummond, who has drawn the president’s ire over his resistance to a planned aluminum smelter in Oklahoma.

As the Sooner State’s attorney general, Drummond filed a lawsuit to block the plant, a Trump-backed project that would be the largest facility of its kind in the country. Opponents argue that the proposal threatens local residents and lands and would give too much control to the Dubai-based Emirates Global Aluminum.

Mazzei once criticized the plan , according to Oklahoma Watch, but has since championed it.

Trump has also suggested that Drummond was not supportive enough during his impeachments, and he accused the gubernatorial hopeful of having donated to former President Biden and the anti-Trump Lincoln Project. Drummond’s campaign has explained that the donations were made in his wife’s name, according to The Frontier’s reporting .

“I respect President Trump and the work he is doing for our country, but we are not going to agree on every issue. I am a conservative Republican, and I believe part of leadership is having the courage to stand your ground when it is in the best interest of the people you serve,” Drummond said in a statement shared with The Hill.

“On the aluminum smelter, the President and I simply disagree. My responsibility as Attorney General is to protect Oklahoma’s land, water and people, and that is exactly what I will continue to do,” Drummond said.

Meanwhile, the run-up to the runoff has been a bitter back-and-forth between the Republican rivals. Mazzei released a drug test this week after public pressure from Drummond, who did the same. The test was negative, according to the Oklahoma Voice , though Drummond accused his rival of attempting to mislead voters by only completing one type of test.

The Hill has also reached out to Mazzei’s campaign for comment.

Trump’s endorsement is a major get for Republican candidates, especially in a red stronghold like Oklahoma.

The Sooner State went to Trump by more than 30 percentage points in each of his three presidential elections, and Republicans dominate the House and Senate delegations. The governor’s mansion has had some more variation — though the last Democrat was elected in 2006 when then-Gov. Brad Henry (D) won reelection in a landslide.

But Trump’s approval numbers have ticked down slightly in the state, as well as nationally.

A survey from McFerron’s firm found that Trump was “still very strong” among Oklahoma Republicans but appeared “clearly damaged” by his support for the aluminum smelter — as well as by his now-rescinded endorsement of Jackson Lahmeyer, a Tulsa pastor who withdrew from a House runoff amid a texting scandal this year.

The survey also found that just 38 percent of Oklahoma Republicans identify themselves as “Trump Republicans,” while a 56-percent majority prefer the label of “Traditional Republican.”

McKee suggested that breakdown “really speaks to the short-term environment” as the president’s popularity dips.

“If that poll is representative, then it would make sense to say Drummond might be the one who finishes first, because clearly there’s more people who say they’re traditional, and obviously, more of those people are voting for Drummond than Maisie,” McKee added.

Sparse polling has signaled the runoff a dead heat . Prediction markets currently favor Mazzei.

And Oklahoma isn’t the only test for Trump on Tuesday as the primary calendar enters its home stretch.

Over in South Carolina, he’s endorsed Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) — who was appointed to fill her late brother Sen. Lindsey Graham’s (R-S.C.) Senate vacancy — against Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) in a special primary runoff for a full term in the seat.

The president has boasted a strong endorsement scorecard throughout the cycle, but his picks have fallen notably short in five gubernatorial primaries in recent months.

Georgia Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, Iowa Rep. Randy Feenstra, Wyoming Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder and Minnesota businessman Mike Lindell all lost out in their GOP primaries . After his initial pick for South Carolina governor, Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette (R), fell into a runoff, he issued a double endorsement for her rival Alan Wilson, who went on to win .

“When it comes to federal offices, the Trump endorsement is very, very valuable. … I think it also makes a big difference in down ballot races on a state level where there’s not a lot of information,” McFerron said, pointing to Trump’s field-clearing endorsement of Rep. Kevin Hern (R) for Oklahoma’s Senate opening.

But the governor’s mansion is “a different issue,” he argued.

“For governor, I think it’s a different issue in that I think voters in states want to have a more personal connection with the governor, and I think anybody’s endorsement means less in a gubernatorial contest than it does in others.”

articles.title: Virginia may be building a national model for corrections
articles.summary: Public safety is not measured only by the number of people sent to prison.
articles.body:
For years, America’s criminal justice debate has been defined by the false choices of supporting correctional officers, being tough on crime and prioritizing punishment, versus supporting incarcerated people, investing in rehabilitation and prioritizing second chances. Virginia is demonstrating that effective public safety requires all of the above.

During Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s (D) first months in office, Virginia has reported a 56 percent reduction in serious assaults on correctional staff, a 47 percent decline in confirmed overdoses and a 27 percent reduction in facility lockdowns compared with the same period a year earlier. Those numbers represent safer workplaces for correctional officers, safer institutions and a stronger foundation for rehabilitation.

But statistics alone do not explain what is happening. They reflect a broader shift in philosophy. Rather than treating corrections solely as a system of confinement, Virginia is increasingly treating it as an essential part of its public safety strategy.

The reforms announced over the last several months tell a consistent story. The commonwealth recently expanded its Intensive Reentry Program into Red Onion State Prison, among the first maximum-security prisons in the nation to implement a program of its kind. It created the Governor’s Community Partnership Council on Corrections to bring together correctional officers, victims, law enforcement, former inmates, families, faith leaders and community organizations to advise state leaders.

Spanberger also restored the civil rights of more than 66,000 Virginians who have completed their felony sentences, allowing them to vote, serve on juries, seek public office and more fully participate in civic life.

Viewed individually, these initiatives may appear unrelated. Viewed together, they represent an effort to rethink what public safety looks like after a conviction. Spanberger summarized that vision when announcing the expansion of reentry programming at Red Onion.

“Reentry programming should not stop at the doors of our maximum-security facilities,” she said . “Long-term public safety requires preparing individuals for a successful, lawful return to their communities, regardless of where they serve their sentence.”

That statement recognizes a simple reality. Nearly everyone incarcerated in Virginia today will eventually return to a community somewhere in the commonwealth. The question is not whether they will return. The question is whether they return with the tools to succeed.

My father spent 33 years working for the Virginia Department of Corrections, beginning as a correctional officer and retiring as an assistant superintendent. Through him, I learned that prisons are not isolated from society. They are workplaces. They are communities. They are institutions charged with protecting both the people who work inside them and the public beyond their walls.

Correctional officers deserve to return home safely every day. Victims deserve justice and fewer future victims. Families deserve hope. Communities deserve safer neighborhoods. Those goals reinforce one another. A prison that is safer for staff is more likely to be safer for those incarcerated. Effective rehabilitation reduces the likelihood of future crime. Successful reentry lowers the human and financial costs of recidivism.

Virginia’s new Community Partnership Council reflects another valuable principle: Good corrections policy should not come solely from politicians or agency executives. Correctional officers understand institutional realities. Victims understand the lasting impact of crime. Families understand the challenges of maintaining relationships during incarceration. Formerly incarcerated Virginians understand the barriers to rebuilding their lives. Local organizations understand what support exists — or does not exist — once someone returns home.

As Spanberger said when announcing the council, she wants to hear directly from all of those closest to the system. This is not a sign of weakness, but one of the strongest forms of accountability. The restoration of civil rights for more than 66,000 Virginians reflects that same philosophy. Restoring the right to vote does not erase a criminal conviction. It recognizes that once someone has completed a sentence, successful reintegration is strengthened when people are encouraged to become active participants in civic life rather than permanent outsiders.

Virginia’s early progress is encouraging, but maintaining it will require sustained commitment. The commonwealth should continue expanding evidence-based cognitive behavioral programming and reentry services to additional facilities. It should invest further in recruiting, retaining and supporting correctional officers, whose safety remains fundamental to any successful reform effort.

The new Community Partnership Council should publish regular public recommendations and annual progress reports, so Virginians can measure whether reforms are achieving their goals. And the administration should continue tracking and publicly reporting outcomes such as assaults, overdoses, recidivism, staffing levels and successful reentry, so policy is guided by evidence rather than politics.

Public safety is not measured only by the number of people sent to prison. It is measured by whether correctional officers return home safely, whether victims are protected, whether fewer people commit new crimes and whether those who have completed their sentences are prepared to become productive members of their communities.

Virginia has not solved every challenge facing its correctional system, but it is asking the right questions. If it continues on this path, it will not simply improve its prisons. It may become a national model for what smart public safety looks like.

Jeff Bennett is the author of “The Black Belt of Virginia: Untold Stories of African American History,” published by The History Press.

articles.title: Johnson: Kushner ‘not directly involved’ in Trump administration after reported meeting with Jeffries
articles.summary: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) on Sunday downplayed the reported meeting between Jared Kushner and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.). “I don’t know what that’s about. I know Jared has interest in lots of other things going on,” Johnson told host Peter Doocy on Fox News’s “The Sunday Briefing.” “He’s not really directly involved in…
articles.body:
Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) on Sunday downplayed the reported meeting between Jared Kushner and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.).

“I don’t know what that’s about. I know Jared has interest in lots of other things going on,” Johnson told host Peter Doocy on Fox News’s “The Sunday Briefing.”

“He’s not really directly involved in the admin, at least in the day-to-day in the White House,” the Louisiana Republican added of Kushner, who is also President Trump’s son-in-law.

The New York Times reported Sunday that Kushner and Jeffries recently met in New York City to talk about areas of common ground.

Kushner has served as his father-in-law’s foreign envoy, focusing on the conflicts in Ukraine and Gaza, as well as failed peace talks with Iranian officials.

The two men reportedly discussed housing, immigration and the cost of living as potential areas of collaboration between the Trump administration and a Democratic-led House.

As of Friday, Decision Desk HQ gives Democrats a 66 percent chance to take back control of the lower chamber. Jeffries has led the House Democratic Caucus since January 2023, succeeding retiring Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.).

During their conversation, Kushner told Jeffries he should meet with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, two people with knowledge of the meeting told the Times.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

In response to comments about the meeting, Jeffries said, “Throughout this Congress, Republicans have adopted a my-way-or-the-highway approach to governing that has failed the American people. To stop the madness, we have repeatedly made clear that an extremist approach will not work and will be met with forceful opposition.”

He added, “The American people want bold change and that’s what House Democrats will deliver. In every conversation that we have with the Trump administration, we will continue to make it explicitly clear that the affordability crisis is not a hoax and nothing short of transformational policy change is acceptable. We are fighting for an affordable America. The question is whether Republicans will join us.”

Jeffries has frequently criticized Trump and his administration over the last 19-plus months, particularly over the cost of living.

Over the last four days alone, Jeffries has called the Medicaid cuts resulting from the GOP-backed One Big Beautiful Bill “devastating,” the Iran conflict “Operation Epic Failure” and Republicans “phonies” for adding to the national debt — which surpassed $40 trillion this week.

While Trump mocked Jeffries last year with an AI-generated video of the latter wearing a sombrero, he told Punchbowl News earlier this month the New York Democrat is a “nice guy” with whom he could do business.

Asked about the reported Kushner-Jeffries meeting during an appearance on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday,” Rep. Beth Van Duyne (R-Texas) said she talks to her Democratic colleagues “all the time.”

“People complain that we don’t talk enough. I think this is showing that the administration is trying to strike deals,” she told host Chris Stirewalt.

“They are trying to come up with compromises. Congratulate them for that. It seems like they can’t win for losing. If they talk to Democrats, they get criticized. If they don’t talk to Democrats, they get criticized.”

articles.title: American Federation of Teachers launches boycott against Target, claims retailer 'remained silent' on ICE
articles.summary: Randi Weingarten launched an AFT back-to-school boycott of Target over ICE silence, but critics say pension fund leverage warrants a federal probe.
articles.body:
American Federation of Teachers (AFT) President Randi Weingarten promoted a nationwide back-to-school boycott of retail giant Target over the weekend because the company had not condemned ICE operations in Minnesota — the location of its headquarters — prompting criticism from education advocates and a call for federal scrutiny.

"We gave Target ample time to stand with the communities in which they operate and help their neighbors, but its silence about federal immigration abuses has been deafening," Weingarten said in a statement.

"The issue could not be more pressing: Seven months since the murders of Alex Pretti and Renée Good, masked ICE agents are still in our streets, our schools and our communities, terrorizing families in the name of Donald Trump's illegal and immoral assault on immigrants striving for their American Dream," she continued. "That's why we're urging our members to avoid Target and patronize more ethical shopping alternatives this back-to-school season."

Weingarten also shared a video on Instagram , where she directed families to the AFT's "Shop Smart, Not Target" website , which maps local back-to-school shopping alternatives. The organization launched the campaign Wednesday after sending Target CEO Michael Fiddelke letters in February and March.

Watch: Weingarten Gestures Wildly During Anti-trump Rant, Later Says He Drives Her To Drink

In a statement to Fox News Digital, DHS rejected the AFT's characterization of ICE.

"ICE enforces federal immigration laws, protects public safety, and conducts enforcement pursuant to federal laws and applicable agency policies. Target is not a sensitive location," an ICE spokesperson said. "However, the current policy provides guidance for officers and recognizes that enforcement actions in or near protected areas require consideration of the circumstances and applicable law. ICE will continue to conduct lawful actions wherever necessary to protect the American people."

The spokesperson further said that ICE did not target schools and called AFT's statement a false narrative.

"This is just another false narrative to try and demonize our brave ICE law enforcement, who are facing a 1,300% increase in assaults against them and an 8,000% increase in death threats," the spokesperson said.

"ICE is not going to schools to arrest children—we are protecting children. Criminals are no longer able to hide in America's schools to avoid arrest. The Trump Administration will not tie the hands of our brave law enforcement and instead trusts them to use common sense. If a dangerous illegal alien felon were to flee into a school, or a child sex offender is working as an employee, there may be a situation where an arrest is made to protect public safety," they said.

"ICE's position remains straightforward: its officers enforce the immigration laws enacted by Congress and carry out the agency's mission to protect national security and public safety. ICE is engaged in targeted law enforcement operations to apprehend and remove aliens in the country unlawfully and will continue to do so despite grandstanding by politicians and criminal illegal alien supporters," the spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "Aliens placed into removal proceedings receive due process. Once it is exhausted, ICE carries out the removal order. Dangerous rhetoric from politicians and activists demonizing our brave ICE officers has led to the over 8,000% increase in threats against DHS law enforcement who are heroically performing their congressionally mandated mission to remove criminal illegal aliens from communities across the country."

Teachers Union Facing Years Of Deficits Seeks To Become Oregon's Largest Pac, Internal Documents Show

Corey DeAngelis, a Heritage Foundation research fellow, told Fox News Digital Sunday that using the organization's pension influence against Target raised fiduciary concerns and warranted a federal investigation.

"This partisan war on Target smells like a breach of fiduciary duty given that AFT members' pension funds own 6.79 million shares of Target stock, which Weingarten has already leveraged to pressure the company into opposing ICE," he said. "The Department of Justice should open an investigation into the AFT using their pension funds and political influence to bully companies into falling in line with their socialist agenda."

"Urging educators and families to avoid Target is not an appropriate use of the union's resources or influence," he added.

This isn't the AFT's first time batting against the retail giant.

DeAngelis also supplied Fox News Digital with a chart tracking Target's closing share price against several AFT actions, including Weingarten's letters and the organization's March boycott resolution.

Sonja Shaw, a candidate for California superintendent of public instruction and Chino Valley Unified School District board president, told Fox News Digital on Sunday that labor leaders were prioritizing political power while students continued to struggle academically.

"Teachers' unions are supposed to fight for teachers. Instead, union leadership has become a political machine obsessed with money, power and influence while our children continue to fall behind," she said. "In California, more than half our students are not proficient in basic reading and math. When a system produces those results year after year, that isn't success. That's education malpractice ."

California's latest statewide assessments showed 48.8% of students met or exceeded English language arts standards and 37.3% met or exceeded math standards.

The AFT's March resolution explicitly called the effort a boycott and urged its 1.8 million members, families and allies to avoid Target until the company stood with the Twin Cities.

Texas' Largest School District Sees Test Scores Soar After State Takeover Despite Racism Claims

DeAngelis' request followed the July appeal by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., for the Labor Department to investigate whether AFT leaders coordinated with retirement-plan fiduciaries to use members' assets for political objectives.

House lawmakers separately demanded answers about reports that member dues helped finance Weingarten's book, "Why Fascists Fear Teachers," while she received royalties.

Teachers spend an average of $895 of their own money every year on supplies their students need, according to a 2025 teacher spending survey .

Fox News Digital reached out to the AFT and Target for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

articles.title: El-Sayed under fire online after taking aim at Usha Vance, female Trump aide in weekend social media posts
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed's post about Usha Vance and JD Vance's grandfather sparked accusations of racism and sexism from Rep. Brandon Gill and others.
articles.body:
The internet is ablaze after controversial socialist Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan invoked second lady Usha Vance in taking a dig at Vice President JD Vance, leading some top voices to question how he would treat female staff should he win in November.

"El Sayed is now attacking Wives [sic] of US leaders? What a guy," said former Florida state Rep. Ben Graber on X .

El-Sayed, running against Republican former Congressman Mike Rogers , launched the attack on Saturday after Vance slammed him for his stated adherence to Sharia law during a rally in Ohio, suggesting the practice would be completely alien to his grandfather, whom he calls his "Papaw."

Vance Unloads On El-sayed Over Sharia Remarks: 'That's Not My Grandpa's Democratic Party'

"So do we think JD is taking Usha with him back in time to meet Papaw, or no…" El-Sayed said, seemingly in reference to the second lady's Indian ethnicity.

El-Sayed's campaign did not return a comment request from Fox News Digital asking him to explain exactly what he was implying.

Swing-state Dem Candidate's 'Disgusting' Comments About Jd, Usha Vance's 'Brown Children' Sparks Outrage

"Why does Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed just assume that all White midwestern grandparents are racist?" asked Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, in response to the post.

"If you're a rural White American living in Michigan, just remember El-Sayed believes you're a racist," said commentator Ryan Girdusky.

Michigan Democrat Accuses Abdul El-sayed Of 'Deeply Sexist Attacks' On Female Political Rivals

"This is why there were ads in the primary correctly highlighting how sexist and misogynistic Abdul is," said an X account run by Democrats supporting El-Sayed's opponent Mike Rogers. "He has so much contempt for women. If you're over the politics of division. Reject Abdul El-Sayed."

Others accused El-Sayed of being racist himself.

White House Tears Into Ossoff With Brutal Takedown After Jab At Key Trump Aide: 'Lightweight Loser'

"You are a racist creep," said journalist Emily Schrader in response to El-Sayed's post.

Earlier in the day, El-Sayed also made a post directed toward Natalie Harp , an aide to President Donald Trump . Far-left media and Democrats online have spent the past two weeks implying that Harp and Trump have an improper relationship.

"Natalie, I think he's had a little too much iPad for the week. He needs his rest," El-Sayed said in response to Trump blasting him at a rally for campaigning with far-left socialist Hasan Piker, who has said that "America deserved 9/11."

El-sayed Dares Gop Rival To No-pads Football Showdown As Senate Feud Turns Personal

"This is what I'm talking about," said GOP strategist Matt Whitlock, posting screenshots of the posts directed at Harp and Usha Vance. "Just a bad campaign, bad candidate, bad instincts. Sitting at home on a Saturday morning tweeting bad takes that any normal campaign would shut down."

"He goes after Usha. He goes after Natalie [Harp]. This coward picks on women who are not in his fight. Imagine how he would treat female staffers in the halls of Congress," said Tudor Dixon , a Republican former gubernatorial candidate in Michigan.

Fox News Digital reached out to the vice president's office and a representative for Usha Vance, but did not immediately hear back.

articles.title: I grew up on food stamps. That’s why I support healthier SNAP standards
articles.summary: Moises Arjona, Jr. argues that SNAP policy should restrict the purchase of unhealthy foods to combat rising obesity and diabetes rates, despite a federal court ruling against such restrictions.
articles.body:
Not everyone will agree with my views on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program , but I hope you will hear me out. While I firmly believe that SNAP is an essential lifeline feeding millions of Americans, reasonable standards on purchases are necessary to ensure the program fulfills its intended mission.

Federal policy should prevent SNAP dollars from being used to buy junk food, candy and sugary beverages. Critics argue that SNAP recipients should have the same total purchasing freedom as any grocery customer. I understand that perspective, but SNAP is not a neutral cash benefit. It is a targeted nutrition assistance program funded by taxpayers to improve food security and health outcomes. As such, establishing clear boundaries around what SNAP buys, while encouraging healthier purchasing habits, is fundamental to achieving its mandate.

Where I live in south Texas, we are facing a serious obesity and diabetes crisis. These health issues are not new, but they continue to worsen, affecting individuals, families and communities across the region, not to mention straining our healthcare system. If we are truly serious about addressing these public health concerns, we must be willing to confront hard truths and demand meaningful policy alignment.

Not every SNAP recipient struggles with chronic illness, but far too many do. We cannot afford to ignore this. Decades of research show that regular consumption of ultra-processed foods and sugary beverages contributes directly to metabolic diseases like obesity and diabetes. When taxpayer-funded benefits purchase products with virtually no nutritional value, we miss a critical opportunity to promote wellness. Meanwhile, millions of low-income families continue to fall short of buying adequate amounts of fruits, vegetables, lean proteins and whole grains.

For that reason, I commend Texas for recognizing the problem and taking action. In April 2026, Texas submitted a SNAP Food Restriction Waiver that sought to restrict the purchase of sweetened beverages and candy using SNAP benefits. The intent was not to punish recipients or limit food access, but rather to encourage healthier choices and promote better long-term health outcomes. This was a practical and responsible approach to addressing nutrition-related diseases that impact our communities.

Unfortunately, in June, a federal court ruled that states could not impose restrictions on what SNAP recipients purchase with their benefits. According to the Food Research and Action Center , the court’s reasoning was that “Congress specifically authorized incentive-based strategies to encourage healthier eating. It did not authorize USDA to redefine what qualifies as food under SNAP or eliminate entire categories of otherwise eligible foods from the program.”

Although I understand this legal argument, the underlying logic is wrong. The reality is that we already know the health consequences associated with excessive consumption of ultra-processed and unhealthy foods. It is difficult for me to accept that products with zero nutritional value should be treated the same as fruits, vegetables, whole grains and lean proteins within a program that was created to address food insecurity and nutritional needs.

For me, this is personal. I have shared my struggles with obesity, but what many don’t know is that I am also a product of SNAP. During the early 1980s, my family depended heavily on food assistance. As a family of five, we received close to $1,000 per month in what were then known as food stamp benefits.

Like many struggling families, we lacked the nutritional awareness that exists today. Week after week, we filled grocery carts with chips, soda and sugary treats. We did buy necessities like meat, rice and beans, but fresh fruits and vegetables were scarce. I saw firsthand how safety-net programs can unintentionally fuel poor health outcomes when nutritional quality isn’t prioritized.

Despite this setback, I hope Texas remains committed to pursuing policies that promote healthier food choices and improving nutrition. Nutrition education is and will be a must. Unfortunately, SNAP-Ed programs, which provided nutrition and obesity prevention education to millions of recipients, were eliminated as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 . Reducing access to nutrition education while simultaneously battling rising obesity and diabetes rates sends the wrong message.

Diabetes rates in the Rio Grande Valley are not falling; in fact, they are surging . If we are serious about building a healthier future, we must address not just food access, but also food quality and nutrition education. SNAP is a vital lifeline and one I will always defend. We double its value when we ensure benefits are used to buy nourishing food.

Requiring higher nutrition standards is not about restriction; it is about reducing healthcare strain and giving future generations a real shot at long-term health.

Moises Arjona, Jr., MS, is the CEO of Unidos Contra La Diabetes .

articles.body:
Texas Rep. Beth Van Duyne (R) said Sunday that Senate Democratic nominee James Talarico backs policies that would “kill” their state.

During an interview on “The Hill Sunday,” Van Duyne said Talarico is “pretty much a complete DSA candidate,” referring to the Democratic Socialists of America. Talarico has never been a member of the left-wing political group.

“His views would kill Texas,” Van Duyne told host Chris Stirewalt. “I don’t think the majority of Texans are going to agree that we need to think about trans kids all the time, that we need to put all the means of production in the government, that if you are a Christian, that you’re going to hate Christianity.”

Talarico, a Presbyterian minister, has leaned into his Christian faith on the campaign trail while arguing that Christians should not impose their religion on non-believers and those of other faiths.

The Texas state representative has also criticized Lone Star State Republicans for passing a ban on most forms of gender-affirming care for minors and has called for lawmakers to protect transgender children.

Talarico has not, though, publicly supported putting “all the means of production in government,” as Van Duyne claimed. The Senate nominee has called for raising taxes on the wealthiest Americans and corporations, increasing the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour and cracking down on corporate PACs, among other economic proposals.

Van Duyne argued Sunday that despite Talarico’s “crazy views,” those views are not “going to catch on” with enough voters in the state for the 37-year-old to become the first Democrat to win a Senate election in Texas since former Sen. Lloyd Bentsen (D-Texas) in 1988.

Decision Desk HQ gives Talarico a 49 percent chance of defeating Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the GOP nominee.

Election handicapper Cook Political Report also shifted the race this week from “Lean Republican” to “Toss Up,” with less than three months before Election Day.
